audit_comment: The story elements tail pins printed pp. 107-108: the foreshadowing tail (the variety, the player-given invitations, dreams, the fortune-teller, the anonymous message, the town rumors), Mystery (the curiosity motivator, the who-done-it, the secret antagonist with its clue trail - the vampire lair, the campaign mysteries of unknown parentage and the vanished community, the background questions, the dying messenger of Eric of Calrede, the speak-with-dead caveat), Challenge (tailored to player types, the encounter role in game balance - random and introductory light, climactic and milestone to the utmost limits, the Hit Dice and damage rough balance, the tactics and position and luck, the intelligent-play sufficiency, the changeable screen dice), Reward (the accomplishment basis, the tracked count, the during-adventure handouts), Magical items (the one-or-two per level lid, the disposable generosity, the class-directed items, the armed-to-the-teeth warning, the described and named items, the Sathas Sundown sage, the item limitations, the story-part doctrine), Wealth (the drains, the kept XP, the low-value bulks, the rare gemstones, the spending sprees), Discoveries (the pieced-together clues), Gratitude (the high king's debt, the case-by-case extent, the explicit promises, the beggar and barmaid favors), Accomplishment (the intrinsic reward, the good-deed cleric, the free implementation), Experience Points (the adjustable DMG amounts, the landslide penalty, the tentative awards, the restructured system, the optional magic-item XP), and Moral (the consequences doctrine, the cooperation, the killer consequences, the accomplishment-merits-reward, the story-for-a-moral).

banner.title: THE DSG STORY ELEMENTS TAIL, R553: printed pp. 107-108 - the foreshadowing tail (the variety principle - corridor after corridor of bloody writing loses impact; the player-given invitations, the augury casting an invitation to the DM for clues; dreams effective but heavy-handed; the fortune-teller's dire warning; the anonymous message; town rumors); Mystery (the unknown as a great motivator of curiosity, the answers a major satisfying reward; the neglected who-done-it structure used successfully; the secret antagonist with a dropped clue every so often - the vampire-lair example with bats and wolves, the slain character with the broken mirror and the pouchful of garlic, the fresh corpse with the distinctive fang marks; the campaign mysteries - the unknown parentage, the vanished community; the long-standing background questions with only a general idea needed, the intriguing hint dropped to launch a fresh story line - the ragged dying messenger of Eric of Calrede; the speak-with-dead caveat); Challenge (the challenges shaped to the players' mental and physical interests - combat for Adventurers with an occasional mental problem, negotiation for Role-Players; the player feedback; the game-balance role of the encounter - random and introductory encounters light, climactic and milestone encounters to the players' utmost limits; the Hit Dice and average-damage rough balance against the tactics, positions, and luck; the intelligent-play sufficiency with logical solutions given a chance; the changeable devastating die roll behind the screen); Reward (based on the level of accomplishment, the count tracked; the tremendous wealth or power destroying campaign balance; the variety of types; the during-adventure rewards - key clues, small treasures, needed equipment); Magical items (one or two permanent items per level; generous with potions and scrolls; the class-directed items - leather armor to the thief, the mace +3 to the cleric; the lid on distribution - mid-level characters armed to the teeth with potent magic killing the campaign; the described and named swords with crest or script; the Sathas Sundown and Black Tower sage; the limitations on every permanent item - the evil-fighting glowing sword, the flame-vulnerable wax statue; the story-part doctrine); Wealth (the taxes, thievery, tolls, and prices as drains; the XP for lost wealth kept; the low-value bulks and encumbrance; gemstones rare until a few levels; the spending sprees with the cleaned-out week); Discoveries (information as reward - advancing story lines, warning of traps; the pieced-together clues the key); Gratitude (the high king's debt; the sincere majority; the case-by-case extent - the paid rescue owing nothing, the careful evaluation of motivations; the explicit promises against requests; the beggar and barmaid favors; selfless motives binding more); Accomplishment (the difficult objective as its own reward for Role-Players; the good-deed cleric; the DM's zero effort; the immediately apparent success or failure); Experience Points (the DMG amounts adjustable - the troll-holding fighter; the landslide village earning no XP and even a penalty; the tentative design awards - 1,000 XP per burned pirate ship, undisclosed until after; the restructured award system for non-treasure objectives; the optional magic-item XP, never for found-and-sold items); and Moral (the storyteller's meaningful lesson, unnoticed if not heavy-handed; the actions-with-consequences doctrine; the social structure's expectations; the cooperation example; the killer consequences - jail, hanging, the fugitive ire, justice catching up; the accomplishment-merits-reward moral; the story-for-a-moral with its 'It's not wise to fool the king' exemplars) - the round ending at the TECHNIQUES OF STORY AND CAMPAIGN DESIGN head.

consts.comment: the magical-item lid: no more than one or two permanent magical items gained per level of experience - the minimum
consts.name: dcfPermanentPerLevelMin

consts.comment: the magical-item lid: no more than one or two permanent magical items gained per level of experience - the maximum
consts.name: dcfPermanentPerLevelMax

consts.comment: the tentative design award: an additional 1,000 XP for each pirate ship burned while on the base
consts.name: dcfPirateShipXP

bools.comment: use variety in the type of foreshadowing; corridor after corridor of bloody writing soon loses its impact
bools.name: dcfForeshadowVariety

bools.comment: the players themselves give opportunities for foreshadowing; the casting of an augury is an invitation to the DM for a few clues about the future
bools.name: dcfForeshadowPlayerInvitation

bools.comment: dreams are an effective, albeit somewhat heavy-handed, tactic of foreshadowing
bools.name: dcfForeshadowDreams

bools.comment: the PCs could encounter a fortune-teller who pronounces a dire warning
bools.name: dcfForeshadowFortuneteller

bools.comment: the PCs could receive an anonymous message from some mysterious source
bools.name: dcfForeshadowAnonymousMessage

bools.comment: rumors picked up in town can also foreshadow events of the story
bools.name: dcfForeshadowRumors

bools.comment: mystery is simply the unknown; curiosity is a great motivator, and discovering the answers can be a major and satisfying reward for all types of players
bools.name: dcfMysteryMotivates

bools.comment: the who-done-it structure is often neglected by DMs but can be used quite successfully
bools.name: dcfMysteryWhodunit

bools.comment: keep the antagonist's identity secret for much of the game, dropping a clue every so often so clever players eventually identify the foe
bools.name: dcfMysteryUnknownFoe

bools.comment: the vampire-lair example: bats and wolves attack, a slain character with a broken mirror and a pouchful of garlic, a fresh corpse with the distinctive fang marks - the knowledge is much more chilling when gained by discovery
bools.name: dcfMysteryVampireLair

bools.comment: mystery as a campaign feature: the character who does not know his parentage, the vanished community raising questions for many sessions to come
bools.name: dcfMysteryCampaign

bools.comment: long-standing questions can lurk in the background; you need not have all the answers, though a general idea helps; drop an intriguing hint to launch a fresh story line
bools.name: dcfMysteryBackground

bools.comment: the dying-messenger example: the ragged battered stranger gasping out a message from Eric of Calrede's father before dying
bools.name: dcfMysteryDyingMessenger

bools.comment: if dealing with PCs who can speak with dead, a different technique is needed for the mystery
bools.name: dcfMysterySpeakWithDead

bools.comment: challenges should be shaped to fit the players' mental and physical interests and abilities
bools.name: dcfChallengeFit

bools.comment: with Adventurers rely primarily on combat encounters and physical challenges, but include an occasional mental problem such as a complicated trap or riddle
bools.name: dcfChallengeCombat

bools.comment: Role-Players often find negotiating sessions or conversations with NPCs challenging
bools.name: dcfChallengeNegotiation

bools.comment: pay attention to player feedback and modify game challenges accordingly
bools.name: dcfChallengeFeedback

bools.comment: a randomly generated encounter or introductory trap should not challenge the PCs too strongly, while a climactic encounter or major milestone should challenge the players to their utmost limits
bools.name: dcfChallengeBalanceRole

bools.comment: a simple comparison of Hit Dice and average damage gives rough ideas of encounter balance, but battles are decided by tactics, relative positions, and luck
bools.name: dcfChallengeHDBalance

bools.comment: plan encounters so that intelligent PC play is sufficient to overcome the challenge; logical solutions developed by the players should have a chance to succeed
bools.name: dcfChallengeIntelligentPlay

bools.comment: if you roll dice behind a screen, you always have the option of changing any die roll that is particularly devastating to the outcome
bools.name: dcfChallengeScreenDice

bools.comment: rewards should be based on the level of the PCs' accomplishments, and the DM should keep track of the number of rewards granted
bools.name: dcfRewardAccomplishment

bools.comment: characters with tremendous wealth or power can destroy the balance of an entire campaign, just as an excessively powerful monster destroys the balance of an encounter
bools.name: dcfRewardBalance

bools.comment: use different types of rewards for different types of accomplishments, and do not neglect any one type in deference to the others
bools.name: dcfRewardVariety

bools.comment: rewards should be handed out during the adventure as well as at the end: key clues showing the players they are on the right track, small treasures, or equipment needed later
bools.name: dcfRewardDuringAdventure

bools.comment: magical items are always welcomed and can be one of the best forms of reward, if used sparingly; be more generous with disposable rewards such as potions and scrolls
bools.name: dcfMagicSparingly

bools.comment: choose items best utilized by deserving characters, either items usable by only one character class or items likely given to certain classes: leather armor to a thief, a mace +3 to a cleric
bools.name: dcfMagicClassDirected

bools.comment: keeping a lid on magical-item distribution cannot be stressed too much: mid-level characters armed to the teeth with potent magic kill the campaign and the DM's enthusiasm
bools.name: dcfMagicLid

bools.comment: permanent magical items should be described in detail; magical swords can be named, inscribed with a crest or script telling of the sword's past or its rightful bearer
bools.name: dcfMagicDescribed

bools.comment: the sage example: an old sage declares 'You carry the blade of Sathas Sundown! You are destined to bring down the evil of the Black Tower!' - the sword's destiny carrying it to a more cooperative bearer
bools.name: dcfMagicSageExample

bools.comment: assign limitations to every permanent item to maintain balance: a sword that glows in the dark and only operates fully when fighting evil, an animated wax statue vulnerable to flame
bools.name: dcfMagicLimitations

bools.comment: make magical items more than high-powered additions to the PC arsenal: a meaningful part of the story, advancing the story and adding to the detail of the campaign world
bools.name: dcfMagicStoryPart

bools.comment: wealth is a standard category of reward, and unlike magical items it is fairly easy to remove excess wealth from the PCs without long-lasting hard feelings
bools.name: dcfWealthStandard

bools.comment: balance the wealth the PCs collect with the expense they encounter: taxes, thievery, heavy tolls, and outrageous prices for goods and supplies reduce the cash characters carry
bools.name: dcfWealthDrains

bools.comment: experience points for wealth that is gained and then lost are granted normally and not lost with the money; DMs must retain a measure of control
bools.name: dcfWealthXPKept

bools.comment: place monetary rewards in large bulks of low-value coins such as silver or copper; carried fortunes encumber, and gemstones should be found only rarely until the characters have advanced a few levels
bools.name: dcfWealthLowValueBulks

bools.comment: the principle of variety applies to wealth: occasional chances to spend money like it's going out of style, with the characters cleaned out a week later and forced into adventuring for room and board
bools.name: dcfWealthSpendingSprees

bools.comment: information can be an extremely effective reward: advancing story lines, answering players' questions, pointing out solutions, and warning about nasty traps or encounters
bools.name: dcfDiscoveryInfo

bools.comment: the key to information as a reward: not completely defined for the players - most valuable when they must use clues to piece it together themselves, adding enjoyment and familiarity
bools.name: dcfDiscoveryPieced

bools.comment: story details and thoroughly designed primary adversaries generate a wealth of information for the players to uncover as the adventure progresses
bools.name: dcfDiscoveryDesign

bools.comment: NPC friendship or gratitude can reward PCs; the high king owing a debt does not harm a character's position, and appropriate situations grow out of the story; in most cases gratitude is sincere
bools.name: dcfGratitudeDebt

bools.comment: the extent of the benefit is case-by-case: a king who paid for a rescue may rule no debt is owed, while unpurchased heroism earns reward and debt; resolve by careful evaluation of motivations
bools.name: dcfGratitudeCaseByCase

bools.comment: a debt may be spelled out clearly ('Anytime you need anything, do not hesitate to call on me!'); without such a promise a request is less likely to be automatically granted, and the king may change his mind
bools.name: dcfGratitudePromise

bools.comment: debts of gratitude are not limited to kings and nobles: a beggar or barmaid spared a threat returns the favor; selfless motives bind more than reward-seeking ones
bools.name: dcfGratitudeHumble

bools.comment: for good players, accomplishing a difficult objective can become a reward in itself, particularly in a campaign with Role-Player participants
bools.name: dcfAccomplishmentIntrinsic

bools.comment: a Role-Player's good cleric gains a sense of reward simply from performing good deeds; this intangible is usually best as an occasional alternative to treasure and magical rewards
bools.name: dcfAccomplishmentGoodDeeds

bools.comment: the DM does not have to do anything other than run the adventure to implement this reward; create adventures challenging the PCs to acts they perceive as valuable, with success or failure immediately apparent
bools.name: dcfAccomplishmentFree

bools.comment: experience points are a game mechanic whose major function is to reward players; the primary measure of level readiness, their distribution requires careful DM planning and adjudication
bools.name: dcfXPMechanic

bools.comment: the DMG's XP amounts may always be adjusted up or down by level of play and accomplishments: the fighter holding off trolls single-handedly earns points for heroism
bools.name: dcfXPAdjustable

bools.comment: the landslide example: characters who wipe out an entire village to slay a single thief get no experience points, particularly if of good alignment - an XP penalty is even possible
bools.name: dcfXPLandslide

bools.comment: tentatively assign XP to potential PC actions as you design an adventure, disclosing such awards only after the adventure, rewarding ingenuity in thinking of the action
bools.name: dcfXPTentative

bools.comment: where treasure-gathering and monster-slaying are not the primary objectives, completely restructure the experience point award system for that adventure; reward good play
bools.name: dcfXPRestructure

bools.comment: whether to award XP for magical items discovered is each DM's decision; if awarded for items found and used, they should not be awarded for items found and sold
bools.name: dcfXPMagicOptional

bools.comment: the moral makes many DMs uncomfortable but using it greatly strengthens a story line; the storyteller shares a meaningful lesson, unnoticed if not heavy-handed
bools.name: dcfMoralStrengthens

bools.comment: the moral simply put: player characters' actions should have proper consequences; the social structure places expectations on its members, and anti-social behavior meets an appropriate consequence
bools.name: dcfMoralConsequences

bools.comment: the most important example is player cooperation within the party: a party unable to agree expends more time and energy fighting each other than fighting monsters
bools.name: dcfMoralCooperation

bools.comment: societies frown upon taking innocent lives; killers must face society's wrath or flee it - jail terms, hanging, the ire of populace and gendarmerie - and justice eventually catches repeat murderers
bools.name: dcfMoralKillers

bools.comment: the challenge-and-reward interaction theme: the moral most DMs impart is that accomplishment merits reward, a lesson quickly lost among treasure gained at little risk or cost
bools.name: dcfMoralAccomplishmentMerits

bools.comment: create a story for the sake of its moral: select the message ahead of time and prove the point - 'It's not wise to fool the king,' 'A thief shouldn't flaunt his wealth in front of those he has robbed,' 'Things are not always as they seem'
bools.name: dcfMoralStoryForMoral

examples.note: the lid: one or two permanent magical items per level of experience.
the tentative award: 1,000 XP for each pirate ship burned.
the foreshadowing tail: dreams and rumors.
the mystery: the secret foe and the vampire-lair clues.
the challenge: the encounter role and the changeable screen dice.
the magical items: the lid and the story part.
the wealth: the drains and the kept XP.
the moral: the killer consequences and the story-for-a-moral.
